deep.reconstruction:
The page holds three unrelated layers.

(A) Historical excerpts, in ink, upper half. They continue the previous page's notes on Gregory (1668) and the Commercium epistolicum (1712). This is material Riemann gathered on the history of infinite series and convergence, plausibly while preparing the historical part of the 1854 Habilitationsschrift on trigonometric series.
(1) 'Additamenta Commercii epistolici ex historia fluxionum Raphsonii (Newtoni opera ed. Horsley, Vol. IV p. 611)'. Raphson's History of Fluxions (1715; Latin edition 1718) appended extra documents of the priority dispute.
(2) Riemann copies Newton's English sentence: 'And am not I as good a witness that I invented the methods of Series and Fluxions in the year 1665, and improved [Riemann/transcription: 'proved'] them in the year 1666; and that I still have in my custody several mathematical papers written in the years 1664, 1665 and 1666, some of which happen to be dated.' This is Newton's priority claim against Leibniz.
(3) Reference 'in Comm. Ep. 523' and 'N° XLVIII' (de Analysi?). Then the note that 'at the end of the copy of this letter Collins had appended: ...'. Then 'Newton to Oldenburg, epistola posterior N° LX, dated 24 Oct. 1676, to be communicated to Leibniz'.
(4) The quoted mathematical claim from the Epistola posterior. Let S = 1 - 1/7 + 1/9 - 1/15 + 1/17 - 1/23 + 1/25 - 1/31 + 1/33 - ... This is the sum over k >= 0 of [1/(8k+1) - 1/(8k+7)]. Newton states S : (1 - 1/3 + 1/5 - 1/7 + 1/9 - 1/11 + ...) = (1+sqrt2) : 2.

Modern verification (mine, not on the page):
- Put A = sum_k [1/(8k+1) - 1/(8k+7)] and B = sum_k [1/(8k+3) - 1/(8k+5)].
- The Leibniz series gives A - B = pi/4.
- The Dirichlet L-series of the character mod 8 with values (1, 1, -1, -1) at n = 1, 3, 5, 7 (the Kronecker symbol (-2/n)) gives A + B = L(1, chi) = pi/(2 sqrt2).
- Hence A = (pi/8)(1 + sqrt2), and A/(pi/4) = (1+sqrt2)/2, exactly as Newton says.
- Equivalently, A = integral_0^1 (1 + x^6)/(1 + x^8) dx.
No derivation of this appears on the page; it is a copied quotation.

(B) Draft on the definition of the definite integral of an unbounded function, in faint ink/pencil, German. Reading: 'If the value of the function does not remain finite everywhere, then integral f ... can have no meaning. If however the function becomes infinitely large only as the argument approaches individual values c', c'', ..., and integral_{c_1}^{c-alpha_1} f(x) dx + integral_{c+alpha_2}^{c_1'} f(x) dx + ... [tends to a fixed limit] when alpha_1 and alpha_2 become infinitely [small], ...'.
- In modern terms: if f is unbounded only near isolated points c, define integral_a^b f = lim over independent alpha_1, alpha_2 -> 0+ of [integral_a^{c-alpha_1} f + integral_{c+alpha_2}^b f]. This is the two-sided improper Riemann integral.
- Because alpha_1 and alpha_2 are independent, this is not the Cauchy principal value (alpha_1 = alpha_2).
- This is essentially verbatim the extension in §5 of Riemann's Habilitationsschrift ('Über den Begriff eines bestimmten Integrals und den Umfang seiner Gültigkeit'). It matches the next page (196r/next), which drafts the localization principle for trigonometric series from the same work.

(C) Upside-down pencil scratch, lower right. The legible fragments are:
- something like x log x + (d/1)(log x - x log x);
- x log x · Prod(1 - d/p) (or 1 - 1/p);
- a sum of bracketed (integer-part) terms Sigma [x/..] ± [x/..] ± ...;
- a product (1 - 1/p)(1 - 1/q)....
A plausible but uncertain reading is a Legendre-type inclusion-exclusion: x - Sigma[x/p] + Sigma[x/pq] - ..., compared with x Prod(1 - 1/p) and log-type main terms. Too fragmentary to reconstruct with certainty. A small pencil sketch of a slanted line is at the bottom.

(D) Upside-down German prose at the bottom left, largely illegible. It is not reconstructed.
errors: In the image the second series appears to be written '1 - 1/3 + 1/5 + 1/7 + 1/9 - 1/11 &c.' The signs before 1/7 (and perhaps 1/9) look like '+'. The correct Leibniz series is 1 - 1/3 + 1/5 - 1/7 + 1/9 - 1/11 + ... This is a copying slip or ambiguous handwriting, not a mathematical claim.
Newton's original wording is 'invented ... in the year 1665, and improved them in the year 1666'. The page/transcription reads 'proved'; this is minor and may be a misreading.

In section (B) the limits are garbled in the hand/transcription ('c^1, c^1' should be c', c'', ...; the lower limit c_1 should be a). The intended structure is clear from the published Habilitationsschrift.

results.what: Newton's 1676 identity: (1 - 1/7 + 1/9 - 1/15 + ...) / (1 - 1/3 + 1/5 - ...) = (1+sqrt2)/2, i.e. sum [1/(8k+1) - 1/(8k+7)] = pi(1+sqrt2)/8 (copied from the Epistola posterior)
results.modern_name: evaluation of a Dirichlet-type series mod 8 (combination of Leibniz series and L(1,(-2/.)))
results.usually_credited_to: Isaac Newton, Epistola posterior to Oldenburg/Leibniz, 24 Oct 1676

results.what: Excerpt of Newton's priority claim (Series and Fluxions 1665-66) from Raphson's History of Fluxions / Horsley vol. IV
Definition of the integral of a function unbounded near isolated points c as the limit of integral_a^{c-alpha1} f + integral_{c+alpha2}^b f with alpha1, alpha2 -> 0 independently
results.modern_name: improper Riemann integral (as opposed to Cauchy principal value)
results.usually_credited_to: Cauchy (1823) for improper integrals; this exact formulation appears in Riemann's Habilitationsschrift §5 (1854, publ. 1867)

results.what: Fragmentary pencil computations with integer parts [x/d], products Prod(1 - 1/p) and x log x terms
results.usually_credited_to: Legendre (1808) if this reading is right

deep.surprise_reason: The ink layers are reading notes from Newton/Commercium epistolicum sources, plus a draft of the improper-integral definition already published in Riemann's Habilitationsschrift. The pencil scratch is too fragmentary to support any claim. The only mild interest is documentary: it shows the historical sources Riemann consulted on series and convergence.

checkable.asserts: Newton's series 1 - 1/7 + 1/9 - 1/15 + ... equals pi(1+sqrt2)/8 (should simplify to 0)
ratio of Newton's partial-residue series to the Leibniz series is (1+sqrt2):2
integral representation of the same series (termwise expansion), equals 0
Leibniz series value used as the comparison series
L(1, chi) for the character mod 8 with values 1,1,-1,-1 (auxiliary step in verifying Newton's ratio)
illustration of the improper integral with independent alpha1=a, alpha2=b around c=0 (limit exists independently of b; equals 2 + 2*(1-sqrt(b)) before b->0, total 4)

transcription_corrections: 'Raphsonii' is correct (Joseph Raphson, History of Fluxions); 'Vlard[?] d. Analysis' is more likely '(Wallis? / Newtoni) de Analysi'. It refers to the item 'De Analysi' in the Commercium epistolicum; reading uncertain.
The second series in the image seems to read '1 - 1/3 + 1/5 + 1/7 + 1/9 - 1/11 &c.' (sign slip in the manuscript). The intended series is 1 - 1/3 + 1/5 - 1/7 + 1/9 - 1/11 ...
'c^{1}, c^{1}, ...' should be read as the individual values c', c'', ... (or c_1, c_2, ...).

The integral is probably ∫_{a}^{c-α_1} f(x)dx + ∫_{c+α_2}^{c'} f(x)dx + ∫ ..., followed by '[einer festen Grenze sich nähert], wenn α_1 und α_2 unendlich [klein werden]'. This matches Habilitationsschrift §5.
'f ... keine Bedeutung haben' should be read as '∫ f(x)dx keine Bedeutung haben'.
The upside-down pencil formulas seem to involve Prod(1 - 1/p) or Prod(1 - d/p) and integer-part brackets [x/p], rather than (1 - d/x). The reading is uncertain.
